authority: UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI) / Sponsoring Employer
form_name: Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS) — issued by licensed sponsor employer
deadline_label: Issued by employer before visa application; minimum 3 months before move date
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employer assigns a CoS reference number through the Sponsorship Management System (SMS); employee uses this reference number in their Skilled Worker visa application.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The employer must hold a valid Sponsor Licence BEFORE issuing a CoS. Licence applications take 8+ weeks if the company has never sponsored before. Most HR generalists don't verify sponsor licence status first — discovering in month 3 that the employer isn't licensed kills the entire move timeline.
non_obvious_action_required: Verify employer sponsor licence status at gov.uk/check-sponsor-licence before committing to any move date. If the company is not licensed, begin the licence application immediately and do not quote a move date until the licence is confirmed active.
source: UK Visas and Immigration — Skilled Worker visa: sponsor a worker

authority: UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI) / Home Office
deadline_label: Submit minimum 3 months before move date; allow 8 weeks standard processing (from outside UK)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Apply online at gov.uk/skilled-worker-visa. Standard processing is 8 weeks from outside UK. Priority (3 weeks) and Super Priority (2 working days) services are available for an additional fee.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The general salary threshold changed in April 2024 to £38,700 (or the occupation-specific going rate in Appendix Skilled Occupations, whichever is higher). Many HR teams still quote the pre-2024 threshold of £26,200 — applications based on the old figure are refused. The going rate is tied to the precise Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) code, and minor classification differences carry materially different rates.
non_obvious_action_required: Verify both the general threshold AND the occupation going rate in the current Appendix Skilled Occupations before offering a salary package. Use the exact SOC code — do not approximate. Check the Immigration Rules directly at gov.uk rather than relying on third-party HR guides which lag official updates.
source: UK Visas and Immigration — Skilled Worker visa: eligibility

form_name: IHS payment receipt (embedded in visa application flow)
deadline_label: Paid as mandatory part of visa application; before visa submission
non_obvious_official_guidance: Pay the Immigration Health Surcharge during your visa application. Current rate is £1,035 per year per adult. Must be paid for the full visa period upfront before the visa is granted.
non_obvious_actual_reality: IHS must be paid for the ENTIRE visa period at application time — there is no refund if the employee departs early, the role ends, or the visa is curtailed. Dependants each pay the full rate. Employers sometimes agree to reimburse IHS as part of the relocation package, but this is not standard practice — the reimbursement agreement must be confirmed before the application is submitted, as there is no mechanism to renegotiate after payment.
non_obvious_action_required: Calculate the total IHS liability for the employee plus all dependants across the full visa period before the application is submitted (e.g. 5-year visa, 1 adult + 1 dependant = £10,350). Negotiate employer reimbursement in writing before submitting. There is no post-payment claims process.
source: UK Visas and Immigration — Pay for UK healthcare as part of your immigration application

step: UKVI Online Account and eVisa Setup
field_label: UKVI Account Email / eVisa Share Code
deadline_label: Account created during visa application; eVisa access confirmed before travel to UK
non_obvious_official_guidance: From January 2025, all visa holders receive a digital eVisa accessible via a UKVI online account. Physical BRP cards are no longer issued for new entrants. Create or link your UKVI account at gov.uk to access your eVisa.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The eVisa is a digital immigration permission tied to your UKVI account — there is no physical document at all. You prove status (for right to work, right to rent, international travel) via a 'share code' generated from the UKVI account, which expires after 90 days and must be regenerated. Losing access to the registered UKVI account email requires a complex Home Office recovery process. Many employees use their company email to register — when they leave the role, they lose access to their immigration proof.
non_obvious_action_required: Register the UKVI account with a permanent personal email address (not a company domain email). Enable two-factor authentication immediately. Generate and save a share code before arriving in the UK — you will need it for the right-to-rent check with your landlord in the first week. Bookmark the UKVI account login URL at gov.uk/get-access-evisa.
source: UK Visas and Immigration — eVisa: your digital immigration status

deadline_label: Must be checked by employer before first day of employment
source: UK Home Office — Right to work checks: an employer's guide

form_name: eVisa share code (right to rent) — generated separately from right to work code
deadline_label: Before signing any tenancy agreement or occupying a rental property
non_obvious_official_guidance: Landlords must conduct a right to rent check before renting to a tenant. Overseas nationals with limited leave to remain provide a share code generated from their UKVI account at gov.uk/prove-right-to-rent.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The right-to-rent share code is generated separately from the right-to-work share code — they are two distinct codes with different purposes and each expires after 90 days. Some landlords (particularly private sector) are unfamiliar with eVisa and refuse to rent to anyone without a physical document. This refusal is unlawful discrimination under the Equality Act 2010 but is widespread and time-consuming to challenge mid-house-hunt.
non_obvious_action_required: Generate a right-to-rent share code from your UKVI account BEFORE viewing properties and meeting landlords — share it proactively. If a landlord refuses to accept eVisa evidence, direct them to the Home Office right to rent checking service at gov.uk/landlords-immigration-check. Document any refusal in writing — it may constitute unlawful discrimination.
source: UK Home Office — Prove your right to rent in England

deadline_label: Completed on or before first day of employment; submitted to payroll before first payroll run
non_obvious_official_guidance: New employees without a P45 from a previous UK employer complete the HMRC Starter Checklist. The declaration chosen (Statement A, B, or C) determines the PAYE tax code applied from the first payslip.
non_obvious_actual_reality: New arrivals from abroad have no P45 — that is a document issued only by previous UK employers. Without a completed Starter Checklist, payroll applies an emergency tax code (1257L W1/M1 or code BR for a second job) causing the employee to lose their personal allowance and pay significantly higher tax from day one. This is extremely common for international hires and typically takes 1–3 months to correct through HMRC. The checklist must reach payroll BEFORE the first payroll run — submitting it on day one of the second week is already too late for that cycle.
non_obvious_action_required: Ensure the Starter Checklist is issued to the new hire before their start date and returned to payroll before the payroll cutoff — not during general onboarding. For an employee arriving from abroad with no UK employment history, Statement A ('this is their only job') is almost always the correct declaration. Confirm this is in the onboarding workflow, not left to chance.
source: HM Revenue & Customs — Starter checklist for PAYE

authority: HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) / Department for Work and Pensions (DWP)
deadline_label: Apply within first week of arrival; number issued within 4–8 weeks
non_obvious_official_guidance: Apply for a National Insurance number online at gov.uk/apply-national-insurance-number. You can start work without a National Insurance number but must apply as soon as you arrive in the UK.
non_obvious_actual_reality: You can start employment without a NI number and provide your employer a temporary reference (letters 'TN' + date of birth) while waiting. However, without a NI number, HMRC cannot match payroll records to your personal tax account, meaning overpaid tax from an emergency Starter Checklist code is harder and slower to recover. The online application includes an identity verification step using the UKVI eVisa account — this is the fastest path. Processing typically takes 4–8 weeks; many employer guides are still based on the old telephone-interview process which was discontinued.
non_obvious_action_required: Apply online on day 1 or 2 of arrival — do not wait until settled. Use the UKVI account credentials for identity verification. As soon as the NI number arrives (by post), pass it to payroll immediately — do not hold until the next natural payroll contact, as each missed cycle extends the period of potentially incorrect tax deductions.
source: HM Revenue & Customs — Apply for a National Insurance number

authority: Local Council (varies by London borough or district)
form_name: Council Tax registration — online via local council website
deadline_label: Register within 2 weeks of moving into the property
non_obvious_official_guidance: Council Tax is a local tax on residential properties. Occupants are legally responsible for registering and paying it to their local council. Register online via your local council — find yours at gov.uk/pay-council-tax.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Council Tax does not exist in most countries — it is a UK-specific annual property tax paid by occupants, not owners, calculated by property value band (A–H). Annual amounts range from approximately £1,000 to £4,000+ depending on council and band. New international hires are frequently not informed about it during onboarding and receive an unexpected backdated bill weeks or months later. A 25% single-person discount applies if living alone. The tax is administered by each local council independently — there is no central HMRC registration.
non_obvious_action_required: Register with your local council within 2 weeks of moving in — it is a legal obligation, not optional. Check whether a single-person discount applies (25% reduction if living alone). Confirm explicitly with your landlord whether Council Tax is included in the rent — it almost never is in private rentals but sometimes is in serviced or student accommodation. Do not use third-party Council Tax sites — go directly to your council's official website.
source: UK Government — Pay your Council Tax

form_name: Bank account application — varies by provider
field_label: UK Bank Account Number / Sort Code
deadline_label: Open within first month; required for salary payment and direct debits
non_obvious_official_guidance: Open a UK current account at a bank or building society. Bring proof of identity and proof of address. Some banks offer accounts specifically for new arrivals without UK credit history.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Traditional high-street banks (Barclays, HSBC, NatWest, Lloyds) regularly refuse new arrivals who have no UK credit history or existing relationship. The practical route for most new arrivals is a fintech current account (Monzo, Starling, Revolut UK) which can be opened via smartphone within 24 hours using passport and selfie verification. These accounts are full FCA-regulated current accounts with valid sort codes and account numbers — entirely valid for salary receipt. Some employer payroll teams have outdated policies suggesting only 'traditional' bank accounts are accepted — this has no legal basis.
non_obvious_action_required: Open a Monzo, Starling, or Revolut UK account on day 1 or 2 of arrival — this unblocks salary payment immediately and buys time to pursue a high-street account in parallel (useful for future mortgage applications). Never delay salary setup while waiting for a traditional bank account. The fintech account is not a temporary workaround — it is a fully compliant solution.
source: Financial Conduct Authority — Bank accounts

form_name: Personal Tax Account — HMRC online service
deadline_label: Check against first payslip (approximately 30 days after start)
source: HM Revenue & Customs — Tax codes: overview

form_name: D9 — Application to exchange a foreign driving licence
field_label: DVLA Application Reference / UK Driving Licence Number
deadline_label: Within 12 months of becoming UK resident for eligible countries; otherwise book UK theory test immediately
non_obvious_official_guidance: If you hold a driving licence from a designated country, you may exchange it for a UK licence without retaking a test. Apply online or by post using form D9 to DVLA.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Post-Brexit, EU/EEA licences can generally be exchanged for UK licences within 5 years of becoming resident — after 5 years, a full UK theory and practical test is required. Many non-EU countries do NOT have reciprocal agreements with the UK: US, India, China, and most South/Southeast Asian countries are not on the designated list, meaning those nationals must pass a full UK driving test. DVLA form D9 requires surrendering the original foreign licence — there is no driving licence during the processing period (6–10 weeks).
non_obvious_action_required: Check the DVLA designated country list before assuming your licence qualifies for exchange. If your country is not on the list, book the UK theory test in week 1 — practical test waiting times can be 8–16 weeks. Do not surrender your licence to DVLA before verifying your country's designation — it will be returned unprocessed if ineligible, costing 6–10 weeks of no driving document.
source: DVLA — Driving licences from other countries

step: Tax Residency and Split-Year Treatment Assessment
form_name: SA109 — Residence, remittance basis etc (Self Assessment supplement)
field_label: Tax Residency Status / Split-Year Treatment Case
deadline_label: Assess in first month; claim via SA109 filed by 31 January following the tax year (5 April)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Determine UK tax residency using the Statutory Residence Test (SRT). If you arrive mid-year, split-year treatment may apply — meaning only income earned after the UK arrival date is UK-taxable in that first year.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The UK Statutory Residence Test involves three automatic overseas tests, three automatic UK residence tests, and a sufficient ties test — it is highly technical and most arrivals qualify as UK resident from the date they start work. Split-year treatment (which reduces the proportion of the tax year subject to UK tax) requires a formal claim via SA109 — it is not applied automatically. Many new arrivals don't claim it and overpay tax in their first year. Additionally, retained ties to the home country (property, family, ongoing employment obligations) may trigger double-residency and require treaty analysis.
non_obvious_action_required: Engage a UK tax adviser in month 1 — not at the January Self Assessment deadline. Confirm whether split-year treatment applies and whether the home country also claims tax residency for the arrival year. Document the exact date of UK arrival and UK employment commencement. Acting early costs far less than correcting an incorrect return after filing.
source: HM Revenue & Customs — Statutory Residence Test (SRT)

form_name: Auto-enrolment notification and opt-out form (if applicable)
deadline_label: Automatic from first eligible payroll run; 1-month opt-out window from enrolment date
source: The Pensions Regulator — Automatic enrolment: guidance for employers

step: Skilled Worker Visa Extension and Role Change Compliance
form_name: Skilled Worker visa extension application (online) / SMS change of circumstances
deadline_label: Apply minimum 3 months before current visa expiry; report role changes within 10 working days via SMS
non_obvious_official_guidance: Apply to extend your Skilled Worker visa before expiry. You may apply from within the UK up to 3 months before the expiry date. Your employer's sponsor licence must remain valid at the time of application.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Any material change to the employee's role — promotion, change of job title, significant change in duties, or salary change that crosses a going-rate threshold — may require a new Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS) and must be reported to UKVI via the Sponsor Management System within 10 working days. HR teams that don't maintain a separate sponsored-employee register frequently miss these events. A missed reporting obligation is a sponsor duty breach and can trigger a compliance visit or licence suspension.
non_obvious_action_required: Set a calendar alert 6 months before each sponsored employee's visa expiry. Establish an internal HR trigger: any change to a sponsored employee's job title, salary band, or core duties must route to the designated sponsor licence key contact for SMS compliance review before the change is actioned. Do not treat sponsored employees as identical to other headcount in HRIS workflow.
source: UK Visas and Immigration — Extend your Skilled Worker visa

step: Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR) — Continuous Residence Tracking
form_name: SET(O) — Application for Indefinite Leave to Remain (online)
field_label: ILR Application Date / Continuous Residence Record
deadline_label: Eligible after 5 continuous years on Skilled Worker route; apply as soon as eligible — no deadline but do not let qualifying period expire unclaimed
non_obvious_official_guidance: You may apply for Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR) after 5 continuous years lawfully in the UK on the Skilled Worker route. ILR grants permanent right to live and work in the UK without time restriction.
non_obvious_actual_reality: 'Continuous' residence is strict: absences from the UK exceeding 180 days in any single 12-month period during the qualifying 5 years can break continuous residence and reset the ILR eligibility clock entirely. Many employees don't track UK absences during the qualifying period — they discover a disqualifying absence at the 5-year mark when nothing can be done retroactively. Extended business travel (overseas postings, frequent short trips that compound) is the most common trigger. There is no UKVI alert — the employee must self-monitor.
non_obvious_action_required: Start a UK absence log on day 1 of arrival, tracking every departure and return. Flag to the employee when any rolling 12-month period approaches 150 days of absence (providing a 30-day buffer before the 180-day threshold). HR should proactively monitor this for sponsored employees as a standard duty — it directly protects both employee tenure and company sponsor compliance.
source: UK Visas and Immigration — Indefinite Leave to Remain: overview

step: Social Security / National Insurance Totalization Assessment
form_name: CA3837 — Application for a certificate of continuing liability in the UK / equivalent totalization certificate
field_label: NI Contribution Class / Totalization Certificate Reference
deadline_label: Assess within first month; review annually if cross-border work continues
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employees working in the UK are liable for UK National Insurance contributions deducted via PAYE. Where the UK has a social security agreement with the employee's home country, contributions may be due in only one country — a certificate of coverage must be obtained.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The UK has social security totalization agreements with several countries (US, Canada, Australia, Japan, and others) that prevent double contributions. For employees arriving from these countries who have recently paid home-country social security, a UK certificate of coverage can reduce or eliminate UK NI liability for an initial period — but it must be actively applied for, it is not automatic. Post-Brexit, the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement has specific rules for split UK/EU working situations that are widely misunderstood by payroll teams. For employees continuing any work in their home country from the UK, the split-liability question requires specialist payroll review.
non_obvious_action_required: For any employee arriving from a country with a UK social security agreement, check whether a certificate of coverage should be applied for before the first payroll run. Engage a specialist UK payroll adviser for any employee doing hybrid home-country/UK work post-move — the cost of getting this wrong (double contributions or incorrect NI class) compounds across all pay periods.
source: HM Revenue & Customs — Social security abroad: NI while working abroad

form_name: SA1 — Registering for Self Assessment and getting a tax return
deadline_label: Register by 5 October following the tax year in which Self Assessment liability arises; tax return due 31 January
non_obvious_official_guidance: Register for Self Assessment if you have untaxed income, including foreign income, rental income, investment income over £10,000, or if you are a company director. Register online at gov.uk/register-for-self-assessment.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Most employees on PAYE believe Self Assessment is only for the self-employed. New international arrivals commonly have foreign income in the year of arrival (final home-country salary, foreign rental income, foreign investment income, share vesting from a previous employer) that creates a mandatory Self Assessment obligation. Failure to register by 5 October carries automatic £100 penalties even if no additional tax is owed. The Unique Taxpayer Reference (UTR) takes up to 10 business days to arrive by post — waiting until January to start makes it impossible to file on time.
non_obvious_action_required: Assess in the first month whether Self Assessment is required: (1) any foreign income in the UK tax year of arrival? (2) share vesting or equity from a previous employer? (3) rental income from the home country? If yes to any, register immediately at gov.uk — do not wait until the October deadline. A UK tax adviser review in month 1 costs substantially less than missed-deadline penalties and interest.
source: HM Revenue & Customs — Self Assessment tax returns

step: Employer Sponsor Licence Duty Compliance (SMS Reporting)
form_name: Sponsor Management System (SMS) — change of circumstances reporting
deadline_label: Report all material changes within 10 working days of occurrence; ongoing for duration of sponsorship
non_obvious_official_guidance: Sponsor licence holders must report changes in sponsored employees' circumstances via the Sponsor Management System (SMS) within 10 working days. Reportable events include: change of job or salary, absence from work for more than 4 consecutive weeks without pay, end of employment.
non_obvious_actual_reality: This is the most common cause of sponsor licence suspension or revocation at UKVI compliance audit. HR teams that do not maintain a separate register of sponsored employees — tracking them distinctly from the general workforce — routinely miss reportable events. A promotion changing the employee's SOC code is a reportable event. A salary increase crossing a going-rate band requires a new CoS. A period of unpaid leave triggers a 10-working-day reporting deadline. Licence revocation means immediate curtailment of every sponsored employee's visa — a catastrophic outcome from a single missed process.
non_obvious_action_required: Maintain a dedicated sponsored-employee register, separate from your HRIS, with columns for: visa expiry date, CoS reference, current SOC code, current salary vs going rate, and last SMS report date. Assign a named Level 1 SMS user with direct accountability. Any HRIS workflow that changes job title, salary, or attendance status for a sponsored employee must automatically trigger a sponsor compliance check before the change is finalised.
source: UK Visas and Immigration — Sponsoring workers: sponsor duties and compliance

deadline_label: Within first month of arrival
non_obvious_official_guidance: Register with a local GP practice; you are entitled to NHS care as a UK resident regardless of nationality. Find your nearest surgery via the NHS website.
non_obvious_actual_reality: GP practices in high-demand areas (London, major cities, university towns) routinely close their lists to new patients. Relocated employees are regularly turned away two or three times before finding an open practice, leaving them without a registered GP for weeks.
non_obvious_action_required: Search for at least three practices near the employee's home address before or immediately on arrival using the NHS Find a GP tool; filter by 'accepting new patients'. If all nearby practices are closed, the employee has the legal right to request registration at any practice within reasonable distance — ask the practice manager directly rather than accepting a front-desk refusal. Use NHS 111 for urgent care in the interim.
source: NHS – How to register with a GP surgery
